danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 16
paragraphs: Fyrst Andrej vidste ikke blot, at han ville dø, men følte, at han var ved at dø og allerede var halvt død. Han var bevidst om en fjernhed fra alt jordisk og en underlig og glædelig lethed i tilværelsen. Uden hast eller uro afventede han det, der skulle komme. Dét uundgåelige, evige, fjerne og ukendte, hvis nærvær han hele livet igennem uafladelig havde fornemmet — var nu nær ham og, i kraft af den underlige lethed, han oplevede, næsten forståeligt og håndgribeligt...
Tidligere havde han frygtet enden. Han havde to gange oplevet den forfærdelige, pinefulde frygt for døden — enden — men nu forstod han ikke længere den frygt.

Han havde følt den for første gang, da granaten snurrede som en top foran ham, og han så den braklagte mark, buskene og himlen og vidste, at han stod ansigt til ansigt med døden. Da han kom til sig selv efter at være blevet såret, og den evige, ubundne kærligheds blomst øjeblikkeligt havde foldet sig ud i hans sjæl, som befriet fra det livets lænke, der havde holdt den fanget, frygtede han ikke længere døden og holdt op med at tænke på den.

I de timer af ensomhed, lidelse og halvt delirium, han tilbragte efter sin såring, jo dybere han trængte ind i det nye princip om evig kærlighed, der var blevet åbenbaret for ham, desto mere løsrev han sig ubevidst fra det jordiske liv. At elske alt og alle og altid at ofre sig for kærligheden betød ikke at elske nogen bestemt, ikke at leve dette jordiske liv. Og jo mere gennemsyret han blev af dette kærlighedens princip, desto mere forsagede han livet og desto mere fuldstændigt nedbrød han den frygtelige barriere, der — i fraværet af en sådan kærlighed — står mellem liv og død. Når han i de første dage huskede, at han skulle dø, sagde han til sig selv: »Nå, hvad så? Så meget desto bedre!«

Men efter natten i Mytisjtji, da han halvt i vildelse havde set hende, han længtes efter, træde frem for sig og havde trykket hendes hånd til sine læber og fældet stille, lykkelige tårer, havde kærligheden til én bestemt kvinde atter uforvarende sneget sig ind i hans hjerte og bundet ham til livet endnu en gang. Og glade, urolige tanker begyndte at optage hans sind. Når han mindedes øjeblikket ved forbindingspladsen, hvor han havde set Kuragin (Anatole), kunne han ikke genvinde den følelse, han havde haft dengang, men han pintes af spørgsmålet, om Kuragin var i live. Og han turde ikke spørge.

Hans sygdom fulgte sit normale fysiske forløb, men det, Natasja sigtede til, da hun sagde: »Det skete pludselig,« var indtruffet to dage før fyrstinde Marjas ankomst. Det var den sidste åndelige kamp mellem liv og død, hvori døden sejrede. Det var den uventede erkendelse af, at han stadig satte pris på livet, som det viste sig for ham i form af hans kærlighed til Natasja, og et sidste, om end til sidst overvundet, anfald af rædsel for det ukendte.
Det var aften. Som sædvanlig efter middag havde han let feber, og hans tanker var overnaturligt klare. Sonja sad ved bordet. Han begyndte at døse. Pludselig greb en følelse af lykke ham.
»Ah, hun er kommet!« tænkte han.
Og det var rigtigt: på Sonjas plads sad Natasja, der netop lydløst var kommet ind.

Siden hun var begyndt at passe ham, havde han altid haft denne fysiske bevidsthed om hendes nærhed. Hun sad i en lænestol, stillet skråt, så den skærmede lyset fra stearinlyset for ham, og strikkede en strømpe. Hun havde lært at strikke strømper, siden fyrst Andrej en gang tilfældigt havde nævnt, at ingen passede syge så godt som gamle sygeplejersker, der strikkede strømper, og at der var noget beroligende ved at strikke strømper. Stikkerne klirrede let i hendes slanke, hurtigt bevægende hænder, og han kunne tydeligt se den tankefulde profil af hendes sænkede ansigt. Hun rørte sig, og nøglet rullede af hendes knæ. Hun for sammen, kastede et blik hen på ham, og idet hun med hånden skærmede for stearinlyset, bøjede hun sig omhyggeligt med en smidig og præcis bevægelse, samlede nøglet op og indtog igen sin forrige stilling.
Han betragtede hende uden at røre sig og så, at hun ville trække vejret dybt efter at have bøjet sig, men afholdt sig fra det og trak vejret forsigtigt.

Ved Troitsa-klosteret havde de talt om fortiden, og han havde sagt til hende, at hvis han levede, ville han altid takke Gud for sit sår, der havde ført dem sammen igen, men derefter talte de aldrig om fremtiden.

»Kan det ske, eller kan det ikke?« tænkte han nu, mens han betragtede hende og lyttede til det lette klik fra stålpindene. »Kan skæbnen have ført mig til hende på så underlig en måde blot for at lade mig dø?... Er det muligt, at livets sandhed kun er blevet åbenbaret for mig for at vise mig, at jeg har levet mit liv i løgn? Jeg elsker hende højere end noget andet i verden! Men hvad skal jeg gøre, når jeg elsker hende?« tænkte han, og han stønnede uvilkårligt, af en vane erhvervet under sine lidelser.
Da Natasja hørte den lyd, lagde hun strikketøjet fra sig, lænede sig nærmere til ham, og da hun pludselig lagde mærke til hans skinnende øjne, trådte hun let hen til ham og bøjede sig over ham.
»Du sover ikke?«
»Nej, jeg har betragtet dig længe. Jeg mærkede, da du kom ind. Ingen andre giver mig den følelse af blid ro, som du gør... det lys. Jeg har lyst til at græde af glæde.«
Natasja rykkede tættere på ham. Hendes ansigt strålede af henrykket glæde.
»Natasja, jeg elsker dig for højt! Mere end noget andet i verden.«
»Og jeg!« — Hun vendte sig bort et øjeblik. »Hvorfor for højt?« spurgte hun.
»Hvorfor for højt?... Nå, hvad tror du, hvad føler du i din sjæl, hele din sjæl — vil jeg leve? Hvad tror du?«
»Jeg er sikker på det, helt sikker!« næsten råbte Natasja og greb begge hans hænder med en lidenskabelig bevægelse.
Han var tavs et stykke tid.
»Hvor ville det være godt!« og han tog hendes hånd og kyssede den.
Natasja følte sig lykkelig og ophidset, men huskede straks, at dette ikke duede, og at han skulle have ro.
»Men du har ikke sovet,« sagde hun og undertrykte sin glæde. »Prøv at sove... vær sød!«

Han trykkede hendes hånd og slap den, og hun gik tilbage til stearinlyset og satte sig i sin forrige stilling. To gange vendte hun sig og så på ham, og hendes øjne mødte hans, der strålede mod hende. Hun satte sig et stykke for på sit strikketøj og besluttede ikke at vende sig, før det var færdigt.
Snart lukkede han virkelig øjnene og faldt i søvn. Han sov ikke længe og vågnede pludselig med et ryk og i koldsved.
Da han faldt i søvn, havde han stadig tænkt over det emne, der nu altid optog hans sind — om liv og død, og hovedsageligt om død. Han følte sig nærmere ved den.
»Kærlighed? Hvad er kærlighed?« tænkte han.

»Kærlighed forhindrer døden. Kærlighed er liv. Alt, alt hvad jeg forstår, forstår jeg kun, fordi jeg elsker. Alt er, alt eksisterer kun, fordi jeg elsker. Alt forenes af den alene. Kærlighed er Gud, og at dø betyder, at jeg, en partikel af kærlighed, skal vende tilbage til den almene og evige kilde.« Disse tanker forekom ham trøstende. Men de var kun tanker. Der manglede noget, de var ikke klare, de var for ensidigt personlige og hjernespundne. Og der var den samme uro og uklarhed som før. Han faldt i søvn.

Han drømte, at han lå i det værelse, han virkelig lå i, men at han var helt rask og usåret. Mange forskellige, ligegyldige og ubetydelige mennesker trådte frem for ham. Han talte med dem og drøftede noget trivielt. De forberedte sig på at rejse et sted hen. Fyrst Andrej anede dunkelt, at alt dette var ubetydeligt, og at han havde vigtigere ting at tage sig af, men han blev ved med at tale og overraske dem med tomme vittigheder. Gradvist, umærkeligt, begyndte alle disse personer at forsvinde, og et eneste spørgsmål — spørgsmålet om den lukkede dør — afløste alt andet. Han rejste sig og gik hen til døren for at skyde slåen for og låse den. Alt afhang af, om han nåede at låse den i tide. Han gik og forsøgte at skynde sig, men hans ben nægtede at bevæge sig, og han vidste, at han ikke ville nå det, skønt han pineagtig anspændte alle sine kræfter. Han blev grebet af en angstfuld rædsel. Og den rædsel var frygten for døden. Den stod bag døren. Men netop da han klodsede kravlede mod døren, trykkede det forfærdelige noget på den anden side allerede imod den og tvang sig ind. Noget ikke-menneskeligt — døden — brød ind gennem den dør og måtte holdes ude. Han greb fat i døren og gjorde en sidste anstrengelse for at holde den tilbage — at låse den var ikke længere muligt — men hans kræfter var svage og klodsede, og døren, skubbet bagfra af den rædsel, åbnede sig og lukkede igen.
Endnu en gang pressede det udefra. Hans sidste overmenneskelige anstrengelser var forgæves, og begge dørhalvdele åbnede sig lydløst. Den trådte ind, og det var døden, og fyrst Andrej døde.
Men i det øjeblik han døde, huskede fyrst Andrej, at han sov, og netop i det øjeblik, han døde, vågnede han med en anstrengelse.

»Ja, det var døden! Jeg døde — og vågnede. Ja, døden er en opvågnen!« Og med ét blev det lyst i hans sjæl, og det slør, der indtil da havde skjult det ukendte, blev løftet fra hans åndelige syn. Han følte, som om kræfter, der indtil da havde været holdt indespærret i ham, var blevet frigivet, og den underlige lethed forlod ham ikke igen.
Da han vågnede i koldsved og rørte sig på divanen, gik Natasja hen og spurgte, hvad der var i vejen. Han svarede ikke og så underligt på hende uden at forstå.

Det var, hvad der var sket to dage før fyrstinde Marjas ankomst. Fra den dag antog, som lægen udtrykte det, tæringsfeberen en ondartet karakter, men hvad lægen sagde, interesserede ikke Natasja; hun så de forfærdelige sjælelige symptomer, der for hende var mere overbevisende.

Fra den dag kom en opvågnen fra livet til fyrst Andrej sammen med hans opvågnen fra søvnen. Og sammenlignet med livets varighed forekom den ham ikke langsommere end en opvågnen fra søvn sammenlignet med en drøms varighed.
Der var intet forfærdeligt eller voldsomt i denne forholdsvis langsomme opvågnen.

Hans sidste dage og timer forløb på en almindelig og enkel måde. Både fyrstinde Marja og Natasja, der ikke forlod ham, følte dette. De græd ikke og skælvede ikke, og i disse sidste dage følte de selv, at de ikke passede ham (han var ikke længere der, han havde forladt dem), men det, der mindede dem mest om ham — hans legeme. Begge følte det så stærkt, at dødens ydre og forfærdelige side ikke berørte dem, og de følte det ikke nødvendigt at nære deres sorg. Hverken i hans nærvær eller uden for det græd de, og de talte aldrig med hinanden om ham. De følte, at de ikke kunne udtrykke i ord, hvad de forstod.
De så begge, at han langsomt og stille sank dybere og dybere bort fra dem, og de vidste begge, at det måtte være sådan, og at det var rigtigt.

Han skriftede og modtog nadveren: alle kom for at tage afsked med ham. Da de bragte hans søn til ham, pressede han sine læber mod drengens og vendte sig bort, ikke fordi han fandt det svært og sørgeligt (det forstod fyrstinde Marja og Natasja), men simpelthen fordi han troede, at det var alt, hvad der krævedes af ham; men da de bad ham velsigne drengen, gjorde han, hvad der forlangtes, og så sig om, som spurgte han, om der var noget mere, han burde gøre.
Da legemets sidste krampetrækninger fandt sted, mens ånden var ved at forlade det, var fyrstinde Marja og Natasja til stede.

»Er det forbi?« sagde fyrstinde Marja, da hans legeme i nogle minutter havde ligget ubevægeligt og blev koldt foran dem. Natasja gik hen, betragtede de døde øjne og skyndte sig at lukke dem. Hun lukkede dem, men kyssede dem ikke, men klyngede sig til det, der mindede hende mest om ham — hans legeme.
»Hvor er han gået hen? Hvor er han nu?...«
Da legemet var vasket og klædt og lå i kisten på et bord, kom alle for at tage afsked, og de græd alle.

Lille Nikolaj græd, fordi hans hjerte blev sønderrevet af smertefuld forvirring. Grevinden og Sonja græd af medlidenhed med Natasja og fordi han ikke var mere. Den gamle greve græd, fordi han følte, at det snart var ham selv, der måtte tage det samme forfærdelige skridt.

Natasja og fyrstinde Marja græd også nu, men ikke over deres egen personlige sorg; de græd med en ærbødig og blødgørende følelse, der havde grebet deres sjæle ved bevidstheden om det enkle og højtidelige mysterium, der var fuldbyrdet i deres nærvær.

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 16
paragraphs: Prince Andrew didn't just know he was going to die—he felt himself dying, already half gone. He was aware of a detachment from everything earthly, and a strange, joyful lightness filled him. Without hurry or anxiety, he waited for what was coming. That inexorable, eternal, distant, and unknown presence he had sensed throughout his entire life was now close to him, and through the strange lightness he felt, it had become almost understandable, almost something he could touch.
He had feared death before. Twice he had experienced that terrible, tormenting fear of the end—but now he no longer understood that fear.

The first time had been when the shell spun like a top in front of him, and he looked at the field, the bushes, and the sky, knowing he was face to face with death. When he came to himself after being wounded, a flower of eternal, unbound love had instantly opened in his soul, as if freed from the chains of life that had held it back. After that, he no longer feared death and stopped thinking about it.

During the hours of solitude, suffering, and partial delirium after his wound, the deeper he penetrated into this new principle of eternal love, the more he unconsciously detached himself from earthly life. To love everything and everyone, to always sacrifice oneself for love—that meant not loving anyone in particular, not living this earthly life. And the more he embraced that principle, the more he let go of life, and the more completely he dissolved the terrible barrier that—without such love—stands between life and death. When he first remembered he would have to die, he said to himself: 'Well, so what? So much the better!'

But after that night in Mytishchi, when, half delirious, he had seen the woman he longed for appear before him, and pressing her hand to his lips had shed gentle, happy tears—love for one particular woman crept back unnoticed into his heart and bound him to life once more. Joyful, agitating thoughts began to fill his mind. Remembering the moment at the field hospital when he had seen Kuragin, he could no longer recapture what he had felt then, but was tormented by the question of whether Kuragin was still alive. And he didn't dare ask.

His illness followed its normal physical course, but what Natasha meant when she said 'This suddenly happened' had occurred two days before Princess Mary arrived. It was the last spiritual struggle between life and death, in which death won. It was the unexpected realization that he still valued life—life as embodied in his love for Natasha—and a final, though ultimately defeated, attack of terror before the unknown.

It was evening. As usual after dinner, he was slightly feverish, and his thoughts were unusually clear. Sonya was sitting by the table. He began to doze off. Suddenly a feeling of happiness washed over him.
'Ah, she's here!' he thought.
And so she was: Natasha had come in silently and taken Sonya's place.

Ever since she had begun looking after him, he had always felt this physical awareness of her nearness. She sat in an armchair turned sideways, screening the candlelight from him, knitting a stocking. She had learned to knit after Prince Andrew casually mentioned that no one nurses the sick as well as old women who knit stockings, and that there's something soothing about it. The needles clicked lightly in her slender, quickly moving hands, and he could clearly see the thoughtful profile of her bowed face. She shifted, and the ball of yarn rolled off her knees. She started, glanced at him, and shielding the candle with her hand, stooped carefully with a smooth, precise movement, picked up the ball, and settled back into her former position.
He watched her without moving and saw that after bending down she wanted to take a deep breath but held back, breathing cautiously instead.

At the Troitsa monastery they had spoken of the past, and he had told her that if he survived, he would always thank God for his wound, which had brought them together again. But after that, they never spoke of the future.

'Can it be, or can it not?' he thought now, watching her and listening to the light click of the steel needles. 'Could fate really have brought me to her so strangely only for me to die? Is it possible that the truth of life has been revealed to me only to show me that I've wasted my life in falsehood? I love her more than anything in the world! But what can I do if I love her?' He groaned involuntarily—a habit from his suffering.
Hearing that sound, Natasha put down the stocking, leaned closer, and suddenly noticing his shining eyes, stepped lightly to his side and bent over him.
'You're not asleep?'
'No, I've been watching you for a long time. I felt you come in. No one else gives me that sense of soft peace that you do... that light. I want to cry from joy.'
Natasha moved closer to him. Her face shone with radiant happiness.
'Natasha, I love you too much! More than anything in the world.'
'And I love you!'—she turned away for a moment. 'Why too much?' she asked.
'Why too much?... Well, tell me—what do you feel in your soul, your whole soul—will I live? What do you think?'
'I'm sure of it, sure!' Natasha almost shouted, seizing both his hands with a passionate movement.
He was silent for a while.
'How wonderful that would be!' And taking her hand, he kissed it.
Natasha felt happy and stirred up, but immediately remembered that this wouldn't do—he needed to stay calm.
'But you haven't slept,' she said, holding back her joy. 'Try to sleep... please!'

He pressed her hand and let it go, and she went back to the candle and sat down again in her former position. Twice she turned to look at him, and her eyes met his, beaming at her. She set herself a goal on her stocking and resolved not to look around until she finished it.
Soon he really did close his eyes and fall asleep. He didn't sleep long and suddenly woke with a start, drenched in cold sweat.
As he fell asleep, he had still been thinking about the subject that now always occupied his mind—life and death, and mainly death. He felt himself closer to it.
'Love? What is love?' he thought.

'Love holds death back. Love is life. Everything I understand, I understand only because I love. Everything exists only because I love. Everything is united by love alone. Love is God, and to die means that I, a particle of love, will return to the universal, eternal source.' These thoughts seemed comforting. But they were only thoughts. Something was missing—they weren't clear, they were too personal, too cerebral. And the old agitation and confusion remained. He fell asleep.

He dreamed he was lying in the room where he actually was, but perfectly well and unwounded. Various unimportant people appeared before him. He talked to them, discussed trivial things. They were getting ready to go somewhere. Prince Andrew vaguely realized that all this was trivial and that he had more important concerns, but he kept talking, surprising them with empty jokes. Gradually, unnoticed, all these people disappeared, and a single question—about the closed door—replaced everything else. He got up and went to bolt and lock the door. Everything depended on whether he could lock it in time. He tried to hurry, but his legs wouldn't move, and he knew he wouldn't make it. He was seized by an agonizing fear. That fear was the fear of death. It stood behind the door. But just as he was clumsily creeping toward it, that dreadful something on the other side was already pressing against it, forcing its way in. Something inhuman—death—was breaking through that door, and it had to be kept out. He grabbed the door, making a final effort to hold it back—locking it was no longer possible—but his efforts were weak and clumsy, and the door, pushed from behind by that terror, opened and closed again.
Once more it pushed from outside. His last superhuman efforts were useless, and both halves of the door swung silently open. It entered. It was death. And Prince Andrew died.
But at the very instant he died, Prince Andrew remembered that he was asleep, and at the very instant he died, making an effort, he woke up.

'Yes, that was death! I died—and woke up. Yes, death is an awakening!' And suddenly everything grew light in his soul, and the veil that had hidden the unknown was lifted from his inner vision. He felt as though powers that had been trapped within him were now released, and that strange lightness never left him again.
When he woke in a cold sweat and stirred on the couch, Natasha came to him and asked what was wrong. He didn't answer and looked at her strangely, without understanding.

That was what had happened two days before Princess Mary's arrival. From that day, as the doctor put it, the wasting fever turned malignant. But what the doctor said didn't concern Natasha—she could see the terrible spiritual symptoms that were far more convincing to her.

From that day onward, an awakening from life came to Prince Andrew alongside his awakening from sleep. And compared to the length of life, it didn't seem any slower to him than waking from sleep compared to the length of a dream.
There was nothing terrible or violent in this comparatively slow awakening.

His last days and hours passed in an ordinary, simple way. Both Princess Mary and Natasha, who never left him, felt this. They didn't weep or shudder, and during those final days they felt they were no longer tending to him—he was already gone—but to what most closely reminded them of him: his body. Both felt this so strongly that the outward, terrible side of death didn't touch them, and they didn't feel the need to feed their grief. They didn't cry in his presence or out of it, and they never talked to each other about him. They felt that no words could express what they understood.
They both watched him sinking slowly and quietly, deeper and deeper away from them, and they both knew it had to be this way, and that it was right.

He made his confession and received communion. Everyone came to say goodbye. When they brought his son to him, he pressed his lips to the boy's face and turned away—not because it was hard or sad (Princess Mary and Natasha understood that), but simply because he thought it was all that was required of him. When they told him to bless the boy, he did what was asked and looked around as if wondering whether there was anything else he should do.
When the last convulsions of the body, which the spirit was leaving, came, Princess Mary and Natasha were there.

'Is it over?' said Princess Mary, after his body had lain motionless for a few minutes, growing cold before them. Natasha went up, looked at the dead eyes, and hurried to close them. She closed them but didn't kiss them—instead she pressed herself against what reminded her most of him: his body.
'Where has he gone? Where is he now?...'
When the body, washed and dressed, lay in the coffin on a table, everyone came to say goodbye, and they all wept.

Little Nikolai cried because his heart was torn by painful confusion. The countess and Sonya cried from pity for Natasha and because he was gone. The old count cried because he felt that before long, he too would have to take that same terrible step.

Natasha and Princess Mary wept too, but not from personal grief. They wept with a reverent, softening emotion that had taken hold of their souls at the awareness of the simple, solemn mystery of death that had been accomplished in their presence.
